title: Is spontaneous human combustion real?
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant examine whether spontaneous human combustion is real. They open with Josh's childhood fascination with the Dr. Irving J. Bentley leg photo, then cover the earliest accounts (a 1663 Paris woman reported by Thomas Bartholin, Jonas DuPont's collection), the typical pattern of victims (torso and head burned, limbs intact, surroundings untouched, greasy residue, sweet smoky smell), and comparisons with ordinary combustion such as oily rags and hay bales. They review theories: Dickens's Bleak House and alcohol, methane in the intestine, static electricity, geomagnetic force, Larry Arnold's hypothesized "pyroton" particle, and the wick effect, where a candle-like fat-fueled slow burn is started by a cigarette or other ignition source. They then recount case studies: Phyllis Nuka in England, Mary Reeser in St. Petersburg, Florida (1951), and Jean Lucille... a 1970s London case where the daughter's flames reportedly came from her mouth. They close with the Fringe TV episode and listener mail about plugging the show and pronouncing Wisconsin.

segments.title: Opening banter and Bentley leg memory
segments.summary: Hosts banter and Josh recalls a childhood photo of Dr. Irving J. Bentley's leg, which shaped his interest in spontaneous human combustion, and a prosthetic leg he saw at a nursing home.

segments.title: History and early accounts
segments.summary: Earliest written account from 1663 by Thomas Bartholin of a Paris woman, then Jonas DuPont's collection of cases. Reports of about two to three hundred cases since the seventeenth century.

segments.title: Defining the phenomenon and typical victim pattern
segments.summary: Distinction between spontaneous combustion of objects like oily rags and hay bales and of humans. Common patterns: torso and head burned, extremities intact, surroundings often untouched, sweet smoky smell, greasy residue, and rare cases of smoldering without flame.

segments.title: Proposed theories
segments.summary: Dickens's Bleak House and alcohol theory, methane in the intestine (rejected because damage is external), static electricity, geomagnetic force, and Larry Arnold's hypothesized pyroton particle, which is unproven.

segments.title: The wick effect explanation
segments.summary: The hosts favor the wick effect: a cigarette or other ignition starts clothing burning and body fat sustains a slow contained burn like a candle; limbs survive because they are cooler, similar to the temperature gradient in a flame.

segments.title: Notable case studies
segments.summary: Phyllis Nuka in England, Mary Reeser in St. Petersburg, Florida in 1951 whose head and backbone remained seated in an easy chair, and a London case where a woman's upper body burned and her father reported flames from her mouth.

segments.title: Fringe mention and listener mail
segments.summary: Discussion of the Fringe TV episode on spontaneous human combustion, then listener mail about plugging a show and the pronunciation of Wisconsin.
